1: An ordinary event can become a scientific question when you look closely.
2: A prediction gives you something to check. Predict when a flower will open, then observe it at different times. Does the evidence support your idea?
3: Clouds become visible when cooling water vapour condenses into tiny droplets or forms ice crystals. Evaporation supplies the vapour; condensation helps form clouds.
4: These questions connect different parts of science. Following water leads from a puddle to the weather. Studying a plant leads to light, air and food. Comparing materials leads to the design of useful objects. Look for these connections as you read. Ask what changes something, and what evidence could help explain it.
5: A useful test narrows the possibilities. Even a new cell needs to be fitted correctly and make good contact. Check those conditions before ruling it out. Keep track of what each test actually shows.
6:
An observation describes what you notice: the clock hands have not moved. An explanation suggests a reason: the cell may be used up. Keeping these separate helps you test your idea honestly.

For a fair comparison, change one thing while keeping other conditions similar. If you replace the cell and free the hands together, you will not know which change mattered. Repeating a check can help you spot a result that happened only by chance.
7: A useful record is specific. Describe which part of a puddle’s edge moved and when. A sketch can preserve details that memory loses. Keep what you observed separate from your explanation of why it happened.
8: Describe an event separately from a friend, then compare your accounts. Did you notice the same details? Which statements describe what you saw, and which suggest a reason? Differences give you something to check together. Finding an answer may need longer observation, a better comparison, or a more precise question.
